entities.name: "Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work" campaign
entities.summary: Chicago-originated (1929) consumer boycott campaign, organized by the Chicago Whip (founder Joseph D. Bibb, managing editor A.C. MacNeal) and activist James Hale Porter with the NAACP. Slogan coined by Bibb; targeted A&P and Silver Dollar Food grocery chains with picketing and daily boycotts to force hiring of Black workers. Promoted the 'Double Duty Dollar' through Chicago churches. First use of direct action among Black Chicago civil rights organizations.
entities.address: South Side Chicago

claims.claim: In 1929, community activist James Hale Porter, Chicago Whip founder/editor Joseph D. Bibb, and Whip managing editor/NAACP executive A.C. MacNeal created the 'Don't Spend Money Where You Can't Work' campaign; Bibb coined the slogan; it targeted the A&P and Silver Dollar Food grocery chains with boycott, daily picketing, informational campaigns, and public meetings.
claims.evidence: Frederick Douglass Opie, 'Southern Food and Civil Rights' (ebook, 2024) documents organizers, slogan origin, and targets; Richard Durham's Illinois Writers' Project essay ('Negro in Illinois' Papers, Box 41, folder 7, Harsh Collection) identifies the 1929–1932 Whip-led campaign as the title subject. Opie notes the Urban League's parallel conciliatory campaign against the same chains and characterizes the Whip's effort as the first direct action among Black Chicago civil-rights organizations.
claims.source: Opie, Southern Food and Civil Rights (Everand ebook); briandolinar.com (Durham essay, Harsh Collection)

claims.claim: The campaign promoted the 'Double Duty Dollar' — the idea that dollars spent with businesses hiring Black workers 'simultaneously purchased a commodity and advanced the race' — through Chicago churches; the slogan was popularized by Virginia Union professor Gordon B. Hancock.
claims.evidence: Papertrell.com (Handy African American History Answer Book) states churches promoted the Double Duty Dollar during the 1929 campaign; Wikipedia traces the term to Hancock. Consistent but thinly sourced.
claims.uncertainty: Term's origin and Chicago-church role not primary-verified; Wikipedia used as finding aid.

claims.claim: The Chicago World's platform (Jacob R. Tipper's paper, 1918–1953) included 'Don't spend your money where you can't work' among its planks, showing the slogan's circulation across the Black press.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Chicago World) quotes the platform plank; consistent with BPM-003's documentation of the competitive Black-press ecology.
claims.uncertainty: Single source; original issue not consulted.

entities.name: "Six-hour dollar" circulation claim (DEBUNKED)
entities.summary: The widely repeated statistic that a dollar circulates six hours in the Black community traces to a 1996 self-help book that names no study; debunked by Howard University's TruthBeTold and economist William Spriggs as an urban myth. Documented as a Disputed claim to prevent the merge step from treating it as evidence — the leakage campaigns are real; the number is not.
entities.address: Chicago

claims.claim: The 'six hours' dollar-circulation figure traces to financial planner Brooke Stephens's 1996 book 'Talking Dollars and Making Sense,' which names no study; economist William Spriggs (Howard University / AFL-CIO chief economist) calls it an 'urban myth,' noting the federal government collects no economic data by religion (the stat's Jewish-community comparator); Howard University's TruthBeTold.news debunked it.
claims.contradicts: Widely repeated by figures including Roland Martin and Boyce Watkins and institutions including Greenwood Bank.
claims.evidence: Moguldom reporting (2023, 2024) on Of Color's blog post and Howard University TruthBeTold investigation, quoting Spriggs directly.

claims.claim: The leakage campaigns themselves are documented even though their quantification is myth: the 1929 Whip campaign, Double Duty Dollar, and Operation Breadbasket all treated Black-consumer-dollar retention as a real, organizable problem.
claims.evidence: See ECON-048 and ECON-001.

entities.name: 63rd Street commercial corridor
entities.summary: PLACE-001's full 63rd Street corpus is cross-referenced rather than rebuilt. Its evidence boundary: Black ownership is documented only for McKie's (6323 S. Cottage Grove) and a Basin Street part-owner; Sears (1929 vs 1934 opening disputed), Wieboldt's at 63rd & Green, and the 'second-busiest shopping district' claim remain unverified. W4's professional-services entities (Henderson, Wylie, Dickerson) address PLACE-001's gap on Black professional services on the corridor.
entities.address: 6323 S. Cottage Grove Ave. (McKie's); 6312 S. Cottage Grove Ave. (Basin Street), Chicago
entities.dates_active: McKie's 1955-1966; Basin Street mid-20th century; c. 1929-1970s; c. 1955-1958 (photographic evidence); Daley's 1892-present

claims.claim: Circa 1955-58, 63rd Street storefronts included clothing, shoe, hat, and furrier shops, taverns, drugstores, a lunch counter, a taxi stand, and a cigar shop (photographic evidence); named firms include Hillman's grocery, Carr's Discount, Robert Hall clothing, Elman's and Kamm & Nate's shoes, Regal Men's Shop, Cottage Grove Rexall, Harrison's Barber Shop, Rothschild Liquors, College Inn, Lauer Sisters, 505 Grill, and Harold's Chicken; Daley's Restaurant (1892-present) is the corridor's oldest continuous business.
claims.evidence: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 research brief and entities, citing UChicago Chronicle (2000), chicagopatterns.com photographic survey, and the Visit Woodlawn brochure.
claims.uncertainty: PLACE-001 grades these Provisional with several addresses still needing directory work; Daley's continuity is Verified in that package.

claims.claim: McKie's Disc Jockey Show Lounge at 6323 S. Cottage Grove (1955-66) was Black-owned by McKie Fitzhugh and hosted John Coltrane and Muddy Waters; Basin Street at 6312 S. Cottage Grove was part-Black-owned by Eddie 'Cleanhead' Vinson.
claims.evidence: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 research brief, citing Chicago Defender citations compiled in UChicago Library's 'Researching Chicago Jazz Venues' guide.
claims.uncertainty: PLACE-001 notes Black ownership is documented only for McKie's and Basin Street's part-owner — not inferred for other 63rd clubs.

claims.claim: PLACE-001's 63rd Street research found Black ownership documented only for McKie's (6323 S. Cottage Grove, still standing) and a Basin Street (club) part-owner; remaining corridor claims (Sears, Wieboldt's, 'second-busiest shopping district') are unverified or disputed, and Black professional services were an evidence gap.
claims.evidence: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 research-brief.md and entities.json (63rd Street corpus, 2026-09-28); W4 inspection confirmed the flagged claims.
claims.uncertainty: Inherited from PLACE-001; McKie's itself was a cross-evidence entity. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

entities.name: 79th Street commercial corridor (Chatham / Greater Grand Crossing)
entities.summary: 79th Street was a major Black commercial corridor of working- and middle-class neighborhoods. Independence Bank, co-founded by George E. Johnson in 1964, anchored the corridor at 79th and Cottage Grove, and the corridor included Black-owned financial institutions, theatres (Avalon/New Regal) and retail.
entities.address: E. 79th St from Cottage Grove Ave eastward, Chatham, Chicago, IL
entities.dates_active: c. 1950s-present (peak as Black business corridor mid-to-late 20th c.)

claims.claim: 79th Street was a major commercial corridor connecting working- and middle-class Black neighborhoods, 'miles of businesses' serving the Black South Side.
claims.evidence: Streetsblog Chicago (2020) describes 79th Street as a corridor where '79th Street connected many working- and middle-class neighborhoods with miles of businesses.'
claims.uncertainty: Interpretive single-source characterization; corridor business-ownership records not checked. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Independence Bank, a Black-owned bank co-founded by George E. Johnson in 1964, occupied the curvilinear building at the southwest corner of 79th and Cottage Grove and was sold to Shore Bank in 1995.
claims.evidence: Newcity Design (2015) identifies the 1964 curvilinear building at the southwest corner of 79th and Cottage Grove as Independence Bank, 'one of the largest and most powerful African-American-owned banks in the country, co-founded by George Johnson... sold to Shore Bank in 1995.' Johnson's 2026 obituary (AP/v103) independently confirms he founded Independence Bank in 1964.
claims.uncertainty: Building date (1964) is from Newcity; bank charter records not checked. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Mid-century Chatham had at least three Black-owned financial institutions: Independence Bank, an Illinois Service Federal Savings and Loan branch, and Seaway Bank and Trust, which provided mortgages on conventional terms to Black borrowers excluded elsewhere.
claims.evidence: Newcity Design (2015) names all three institutions and argues they gave Black borrowers conventional mortgages denied elsewhere.
claims.uncertainty: Single source; 'built Chatham' framing is interpretive; charter records not checked. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

cross_references: CTL-DR-BVM-005 (Avalon/New Regal Theater at 79th — John Eberson design; ownership evidence boundary)
entities.geography_notes: Major east-west commercial spine of the Black middle-class South Side; anchor corridor for the 'later Black South Side' geography.

entities.address: E/W 87th St, Chatham and Auburn Gresham, Chicago, IL

claims.claim: 87th Street Center, a 132,427 sq ft shopping center built in 1974 and renovated in 2017, is a retail anchor of the contemporary 87th Street corridor in Chatham.
claims.evidence: Connect CRE reports 87th Street Center in Chatham, 132,427 sq ft, built 1974, renovated 2017, anchored by tenants including Walgreens and Food 4 Less.
claims.uncertainty: Real-estate marketing copy; ownership not stated. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Chatham Village Square is described as home to the first urban Target and Nike Factory Store, and Chatham Ridge Shopping Center (87th & Lafayette) was built 1989-1990.
claims.evidence: Chatham Village Square listing (Showcase); Chatham Ridge LoopNet listing (built 1989-90).
claims.uncertainty: Marketing listings; claims of 'first urban Target' unattested elsewhere; Black ownership of corridor businesses unverified. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

entities.name: A.B. Molar (Moler) Beauty School / Beauty and Culture School
entities.summary: Chicago cosmetology school whose 1916 graduation of Marjorie Stewart Joyner broke its color line. A training institution in the Black women's beauty economy: the school supplied the credential that let Black women open independent salons.
entities.address: Chicago (street address not verified in consulted sources)
entities.dates_active: Operating by 1916; later history not traced

claims.claim: In 1916 Marjorie Stewart Joyner became the first African American to graduate from Chicago's A.B. Molar Beauty School (also styled 'A.B. Moler Beauty and Culture School').
claims.evidence: Lemelson-MIT Center, Happi, Wikipedia, and the National Inventors Hall of Fame fact sheet all record the 1916 first-Black-graduate fact.
claims.source: Lemelson-MIT Center; National Inventors Hall of Fame 2023 fact sheet
claims.uncertainty: Spelling varies (Molar vs. Moler) across sources; ownership and later history not traced.

entities.name: Annie Turnbo Malone
entities.summary: Cosmetology pioneer and philanthropist; built the Poro beauty empire in St. Louis and moved its headquarters to Chicago's Poro Block in 1930 after divorce and Depression-era losses.
entities.address: Metropolis, Illinois (birth); St. Louis, Missouri (1890s-1930); Chicago (1930-1957)

claims.claim: Annie Minerva Turnbo was born August 9, 1869, in Metropolis, Illinois, the tenth of eleven children; orphaned young and raised by her sister Ada Moody; developed scalp and hair products by the 1890s.
claims.evidence: SHSMO Historic Missourians; AAUW Columbia (MO); Face2Face Africa.
claims.source: SHSMO, 'Annie Turnbo Malone'; AAUW Columbia MO

claims.claim: Malone's empire peaked in the 1920s with multimillion-dollar scale (claimed $14 million in assets in 1920); the 'first Black woman millionaire' title is widely claimed but contemporaneous documentation is thin.
claims.contradicts: Madam C.J. Walker is commonly credited as the first self-made Black woman millionaire; Malone's claim is older but less documented.
claims.evidence: Good Black News (2016): '$14 million in assets held in 1920'; SHSMO: 'multimillion-dollar business empire.'
claims.uncertainty: Tax/asset records not retrieved; the Walker-vs-Malone primacy debate is historiographic, not settled.

claims.claim: In 1927 her husband Aaron Eugene Malone filed for divorce and demanded half the business; the settlement was $200,000. Combined with lawsuits, unpaid real-estate and excise taxes (including the 1920s 20% luxury tax on hair-care products), and the 1929 crash, her finances collapsed: ~$100,000 in federal tax debt by 1943; she lost control of Poro to the government and creditors in 1951.
claims.evidence: SHSMO; LA Sentinel; Face2Face Africa.
claims.uncertainty: Tax/IRS records not retrieved; figures from biographical sources.

claims.claim: Malone was a major philanthropist: president of the St. Louis Colored Orphans Home board 1919-1943; the home was renamed for her in 1946 (now Annie Malone Children and Family Service Center).
claims.evidence: SHSMO; AAUW Columbia (MO), citing Dictionary of Missouri Biography.

claims.claim: Madam C.J. Walker is often described as Malone's former employee/sales agent (met Malone c. 1903). This is widely repeated but rests on limited evidence; treat as provisional.
claims.evidence: Face2Face Africa; LA Sentinel ('there would be no Madame C.J. Walker' without Malone).
claims.uncertainty: Scholarly consensus on the Walker-Malone relationship is unsettled; needs archival verification.

claims.claim: Malone died in Chicago on May 10, 1957; her estate was valued at $100,000 and went to her nieces and nephews.
claims.evidence: SHSMO; LA Sentinel.

entities.name: Anthony Overton
entities.summary: Founder of one of the largest Black-owned business conglomerate of early 20th-century Chicago — cosmetics manufacturing, banking, insurance, real estate, and publishing — builder of the State Street commercial spine of Bronzeville.
entities.address: Chicago (moved 1911); born Monroe, Louisiana

claims.claim: Anthony Overton was born in Monroe, Louisiana — March 21, 1865 per BlackPast and Wikipedia's infobox; Wikipedia's article text gives March 18, 1864. Birth date is disputed.
claims.contradicts: Wikipedia article text: 'Anthony Overton Jr. (March 18, 1864 – July 2, 1946).' Infobox: Born (1865-03-21).
claims.evidence: BlackPast: March 21, 1865. Wikipedia: both dates appear.
claims.uncertainty: Resolve via census or birth records.

claims.claim: Overton earned a law degree from the University of Kansas (1888) after attending Washburn College in Topeka, and was elected a municipal judge in Topeka in 1892.
claims.evidence: BlackPast; Wikipedia.

claims.claim: Overton founded the Hygienic Manufacturing Company in Kansas City in 1898 with $2,000 in family savings (first product: baking powder), survived bankruptcy after the 1902 Kansas River flood destroyed his plant, and moved the business to Chicago's South Side in 1911.
claims.evidence: BlackPast; Next City (2019); BVM-005 entities.
claims.source: BlackPast.org; Next City, 'Restoring the Glory of This Iconic Chicago Black Metropolis Building' (2019)

claims.claim: Overton's conglomerate included Overton Hygienic Manufacturing Co., Victory Life Insurance Company, Douglass National Bank, Great Northern Realty Company, Half-Century Magazine (1916), and the Chicago Bee (1925).
claims.evidence: BlackPast; Wikipedia; Next City (2019); Face2Face Africa; BVM-005 (biz-overton-hygienic-co, Verified).
claims.uncertainty: Ownership percentages and holding-company structure not documented.

claims.claim: Overton won the NAACP Spingarn Medal in 1927.
claims.evidence: BlackPast 'Black History Mini Docs' summary; Wikipedia notes Provisional status in BVM-005 ('needs NAACP records').
claims.uncertainty: Confirm against NAACP Spingarn Medal rolls.

claims.claim: Overton commissioned the Overton Hygienic Building (1922, architect Z. Erol Smith) at 3619-3627 S. State Street and the Chicago Bee Building (commissioned 1929), housing his companies' manufacturing, bank, insurance, real estate, and newsroom operations.
claims.evidence: Next City (2019); Face2Face Africa; BVM-005 (Chicago Bee Building; Overton Hygienic Building).

claims.claim: Overton died in July 1946 — July 2 per Wikipedia, July 3 per BVM-005. The day is disputed; the month and year are consistent.
claims.contradicts: BVM-005 (person-anthony-overton): 'died July 3, 1946.'
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: July 2, 1946. BVM-005: July 3, 1946.
claims.uncertainty: Resolve via obituary/death records.

claims.claim: Commonly described as one of the largest Black-owned business conglomerates of early 20th-century Chicago; the superlative is widely repeated but not verified against comparative firm data in this pass.
claims.evidence: Secondary literature (e.g., Weems 2020 for Overton).
claims.uncertainty: Do not render the superlative as established fact.

entities.name: Best Chicago Meat Co. / Moo & Oink (supplier→brand rescue)
entities.summary: Moo & Oink (originally Calumet Meat Co., renamed 1976) was a South/West Side grocery-and-meat chain (4 stores, 200 employees) that entered Chapter 7 bankruptcy September 2011; stores closed, real estate unsold. Its supplier of 30 years — the second-generation Black-owned Best Chicago Meat Co. — bought the brand at auction ($530,000) and rebuilt it to 300 stores in five states. A supplier→retailer cycle link and a Black-owned rescue of a community brand.
entities.address: Chicago (manufacturer and meat supplier)
entities.dates_active: 1976–2011 (retail); brand continues under Best Chicago Meat from 2012

claims.claim: Best Chicago Meat Co. produced burgers and sausages for Moo & Oink for 30 years before acquiring the brand and intellectual property at public auction for $530,000 after Moo & Oink's Chapter 7 bankruptcy (stores closed Sept 30, 2011; 200 employees; four locations: Austin, two South Side, Hazel Crest).
claims.evidence: Meat+Poultry trade press (Oct 2011): bankruptcy and closures; 127238.activeboard.com (Meat & Poultry staff): $530,000 auction acquisition; Shelby Report (2026): 50th-anniversary history, 30-year supplier relationship.

claims.claim: Best Chicago Meat is a second-generation Black-owned family business (Robert M. Beavers Jr., chairman/CEO); under its ownership Moo & Oink products returned to Chicago grocery shelves and expanded to 300 stores in five states.
claims.evidence: Shelby Report (2026): 'Best Chicago Meat, a second-generation Black-owned family business'; Progressive Grocer: Roundy's partnership carrying Moo & Oink in Wisconsin/Minnesota.

claims.claim: Moo & Oink's retail collapse was attributed to mounting debt and declining sales during the Great Recession; the store locations themselves remained unsold after the bankruptcy.
claims.evidence: Austin Weekly News via scceu.org (mounting debt + declining sales during Great Recession); Wikipedia/meatpoultry: no bidders on the real estate.
claims.uncertainty: Bankruptcy-court findings not consulted; single trade-press attribution.

entities.name: Binga Block storefronts (State Street, 47th-48th) and Binga Arcade shops (35th & State)
entities.summary: Ordinary retail layer of Jesse Binga's property holdings: the Binga Block on State between 47th and 48th hosted a pharmacy with door-to-door Poro product sales and a barber shop; the Binga Arcade at 35th and State housed the bank plus offices, shops, and a dance floor. Documented at block level, not as named firms.
entities.address: State Street between 47th and 48th (Binga Block); 35th and State (Binga Arcade)

claims.claim: The Binga Block, on State Street between 47th and 48th streets, hosted businesses including a pharmacy with door-to-door sales of Poro products and a barber shop; the Binga Arcade at 35th and State housed the Binga Bank with offices, shops, and a dance floor.
claims.evidence: IIT Bronzeville History Booklet (2024).
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; the pharmacy, barber shop, and arcade shops are unnamed — city directories needed for firm names.

entities.name: Binga State Bank
entities.summary: Jesse Binga's private bank (1908), state-chartered 1921, closed 1930. First Black-owned bank in the Northern U.S. Lent to Black homebuyers and entrepreneurs shut out of white banks; employed Black white-collar workers. Its capitalization partly traced to informal-economy wealth (gambling kingpin John 'Mushmouth' Johnson's estate via Eudora Johnson).
entities.address: 3633 S. State St. (1908 private bank, per NPS); later bank building at State & 36th Place (Provisional); acquired former McCarthy Bank building at 35th & State after the Panic of 1907 (Provisional)

claims.claim: Binga acquired the former McCarthy Bank building at 35th & State after that white-owned bank collapsed in the Panic of 1907, launching Binga Bank in 1908; the bank took in over $200,000 in deposits on its opening day.
claims.evidence: Chicago Southsider article on Binga (citing The Broad Ax, Jan. 1, 1910 for the opening-day deposit figure).
claims.source: Chicago Southsider, 'Jesse Binga: The Making of the First Black-Owned Bank on the South Side of Chicago'
claims.uncertainty: Single modern secondary citing a 1910 Black newspaper; The Broad Ax itself is a near-primary source worth direct consultation. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: At the August 1909 National Negro Business Men's League conference in Louisville, Booker T. Washington hailed Binga as 'the most progressive and successful Afro-American banker and real estate broker in this country.'
claims.evidence: Reported in The Broad Ax (Vol. 15, No. 13, Jan. 1, 1910), via the Chicago Southsider.
claims.source: The Broad Ax via Chicago Southsider
claims.uncertainty: Quoted secondhand through a modern article; direct consultation of The Broad Ax recommended. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Binga State Bank closed in June 1930 during the Great Depression. Binga was convicted in 1933 of embezzling $22,000 in bank funds, sentenced to 10 years, and released after 3 following petitions including one from Clarence Darrow.
claims.evidence: BlackPast (Trevor Goodloe) reports the 1933 conviction, sentence, early release, and Darrow petition; BVM-005 corroborates the June 1930 closure.
claims.uncertainty: The embezzlement narrative is single-sourced here and contested in some Black-history accounts; needs 1933 court/press records before publication as fact. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: The bank grew out of Binga's real-estate business serving Black migrants shut out of white lending; he also built the Binga Arcade Building (1929, 35th & State) and financed Black homeownership beyond the Black Belt.
claims.evidence: BVM-005 synthesis (BlackPast, NPS); Chicago Southsider on Binga's real-estate-first route into banking.
claims.uncertainty: Specific lending volumes and terms from Binga's bank records not located; receivership details beyond the 1930 closure are unresolved. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Binga opened a private bank in 1908; it received a state charter in 1921 as Binga State Bank and closed in 1930. It was the first Black-owned bank in the Northern U.S.
claims.evidence: Cross-referenced from CTL-DR-BVM-005 (NPS National Register nomination; Black Enterprise; BlackPast; Kansas City Fed, 'Let Us Put Our Money Together,' 2019). | Also documented via Kansas City Federal Reserve historical account.
claims.source: NPS Black Metropolis thematic nomination; Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (2019)
claims.uncertainty: Consolidated from two near-duplicate claims at merge (F-008).

claims.claim: Binga State Bank offered loans to Black homebuyers and entrepreneurs who faced discrimination from white banks and predatory lenders, and employed Black workers in rare well-compensated white-collar jobs.
claims.evidence: BlackPast and African American Registry profiles assert loans to homebuyers and business founders plus white-collar employment; consistent across secondary profiles but no primary loan-ledger or employment evidence consulted.
claims.uncertainty: Secondary-only; specific borrowers and loan volumes undocumented in sources consulted.

claims.claim: Part of Binga's bank capitalization came from informal-economy wealth: his wife Eudora Johnson inherited over $200,000 in 1907 from her father, gambling kingpin John 'Mushmouth' Johnson, and the money was merged with the bank's capitalization.
claims.contradicts: samepassage.org calls Eudora a 'relative' of Mushmouth Johnson; libertarianism.org calls her his daughter.
claims.evidence: Consistent across samepassage.org, libertarianism.org, and chicagosouthsider.com; Hayner biography excerpt (Northwestern UP, 2019) discusses Binga's real-estate-to-bank trajectory. No primary probate/bank records consulted.
claims.source: samepassage.org; libertarianism.org; Hayner excerpt via WTTW (2019)
claims.uncertainty: Inheritance figure and its transfer into bank capital not primary-verified; relationship of Eudora to Mushmouth Johnson varies ('relative' vs 'daughter') across sources.

claims.claim: Binga State Bank's address is reported as 3633 S. State Street (NPS) and as State & 36th Place; these describe the same vicinity (3600 block of South State).
claims.evidence: W1 (NPS citation) vs W4 cross-reference note.
claims.uncertainty: Exact siting needs Sanborn/directory verification.

entities.name: Black dentists: Ida Gray Nelson Rollins and Olive Myrtle Henderson
entities.summary: Ida Gray Nelson Rollins, the first African-American woman dentist in the United States, moved her practice to Chicago in 1895; Olive Myrtle Henderson, Northwestern's first Black woman dental graduate (1908), was inspired by Rollins, became Chicago's second Black woman dentist, and ran a South Side private practice from 1912 to 1948.
entities.address: South Side, Chicago, IL (practices; exact addresses not verified)

claims.claim: Ida Gray (later Ida Gray Nelson Rollins) graduated from the University of Michigan College of Dentistry in 1890 as the first African-American woman dentist in the United States; she relocated her practice to Chicago in 1895, served both Black and white clients, and practiced until 1928.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Ida Gray), citing University of Michigan and dental-history sources.
claims.uncertainty: Single chain; U-M records not checked; Chicago office address not found. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review. Red-team F-016: Wikipedia single chain; downgrade pending U-M/dental-history source

claims.claim: Olive Myrtle Henderson, inspired by Rollins, graduated from Northwestern Dental School in 1908 as Northwestern's first Black woman dental graduate; she was Chicago's second Black woman dentist, opened a South Side private practice in 1912, and practiced until 1948.
claims.evidence: Northwestern Galter 'African American Medical and Dental Pioneers' (2016): Henderson graduated 1908, 'Northwestern's first black woman dental graduate,' opened 'her own private practice on the South Side of Chicago in 1912,' practiced until 1948; Mortenson Dental Partners (2021) corroborates the 1908 graduation, 1912 practice, and Rollins inspiration.
claims.source: Northwestern Galter PDF; Mortenson Dental Partners
claims.uncertainty: Practice address not stated in sources found; the Henderson-Rollins mentorship is documented through one institutional chain. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

cross_references: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 (63rd St professional-services gap); ECON-W4-015 (Wylie, professional-class parallel)
entities.geography_notes: Medical/dental professionals whose practices were Black business infrastructure; Rollins mentored/inspired Henderson.

entities.name: Black retailers' supply-chain dependency
entities.summary: Black Chicago retailers depended on white-owned supply and distribution chains — from the Madison Street businesses picketed in 1965-66 to distributors sending expired food to Black-neighborhood stores. The one documented Black-owned supply chain in the sources (an NOI grocery partnered with Black producers) collapsed after integration. Whether Black entrepreneurs acquired commercial property through contract selling is unresolved: all documented contract-selling evidence in Chicago is residential.
entities.address: Chicago, IL (corridors and supply chains)

claims.claim: Black retailers depended on white-owned supply chains: the 1965-66 SCLC pickets on Madison Street targeted white-owned businesses over hiring and wages, and the Whip's 'Don't Spend Your Money Where You Can't Work' campaigns (per BPM-003) show the same dependency between Black consumers/workers and white-owned commercial chains.
claims.evidence: ProPublica (2020) on the Madison pickets; CTL-DR-BPM-003 on the Whip's 1929-30s campaigns.
claims.uncertainty: Wholesaler-level supply relations are inferred from the labor/retail pattern, not documented per distributor. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: A mid-20th-century Nation of Islam grocery store in Chicago partnered with Black producers to create Black-owned suppliers; the store collapsed as Black shoppers moved to large white-owned chain stores after integration.
claims.evidence: Civil Eats (2018), quoting Sheelah Muhammad: 'Her father ran the Nation of Islam's grocery store in Chicago... The store partnered with Black producers to create suppliers, building a model of self-sufficiency that eventually collapsed as Black shoppers chose large, white-owned chain stores once integration laws passed.'
claims.uncertainty: Single source, oral-history chain; store name and dates not stated. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Investigative reporting documents a pattern of distributors supplying expired or nearly expired food to Black-neighborhood stores — evidence of racialized supply-chain disadvantage.

entities.summary: Chicago's open-air market (1912 city ordinance), an incubator for low-income and minority micro-entrepreneurs and the cradle of electrified Chicago blues. The track's clearest documented case of urban-renewal displacement of a Black-and-immigrant business district.
entities.address: Maxwell and Halsted Streets (Roosevelt Rd. to 16th St.), Near West Side Chicago
entities.dates_active: 1912–1994 (original site); Late 19th century-1994 (officially recognized 1912; moved to Roosevelt & Des Plaines 2008)

claims.claim: The city created the Maxwell Street Market by 1912 ordinance; it became a thriving commercial hub attracting low-income and minority entrepreneurs, a 'hotbed of entrepreneurial micro-capitalism' where poor people with little skill could start businesses and some went on to start substantial businesses.
claims.evidence: In These Times interview with Roosevelt University economist Steve Balkin; Wikipedia.

claims.claim: Black participation grew in the 1920s-1940s with the Great Migration; Black street musicians became famous there, and in the 1940s Southern Black newcomers worked in Maxwell Street stores while blues performers played on Sundays.
claims.evidence: Google Arts & Culture (Obsidian Collection); UChicago student history (voices.uchicago.edu); Chicago History Museum.

claims.claim: In 1994, over vendor and preservationist protests, the market was demolished to accommodate UIC campus expansion; the market now operates Sundays at Roosevelt Rd. and Des Plaines Ave.
claims.evidence: In These Times; Wikipedia.

claims.claim: A 1912 city ordinance created the Maxwell Street Market where licensed peddlers could sell seven days a week; it became a commercial hub for low-income and minority entrepreneurs — 'a hotbed of entrepreneurial micro-capitalism' where vendors started substantial businesses.
claims.evidence: In These Times (quoting Roosevelt University economist Steve Balkin, co-founder of the Openair Market Network); city of Chicago history page.

claims.claim: In 1966 the city declared Maxwell Street 'a slum and blighted'; UIC received permission to exercise eminent domain (held off for years, depressing area real-estate prices); in 1994 the market was moved to Canal Street over vendor and preservationist protests; its final buildings were demolished in 2002; the area became University Village.
claims.evidence: CityCast Chicago explainer documents the 1966 blight designation, UIC eminent-domain permission, 1994 move, and 2002 demolition; chicago.gov confirms the 1994 move to accommodate UIC expansion and the 2008 Desplaines relocation.

claims.claim: The vendor base collapsed from over 1,200 in the market's heyday to about 35 sellers at the relocated market in 2025.
claims.evidence: CityCast Chicago explainer (2025): 'last year's Maxwell Street Market featured 35 sellers. There were over 1,200 in the flea market's heyday.' Single source.
claims.uncertainty: Heyday figure not dated or sourced in the explainer.

entities.name: National Negro Bankers Association (later National Bankers Association)
entities.summary: Trade association of Black-owned banks and S&Ls founded 1927 in response to ABA exclusion; renamed NBA 1948; the industry's collective advocate; Bronzeville's banks operated within its orbit.
entities.address: Founded in Durham, North Carolina (1927); headquartered Washington, D.C. (later)

claims.claim: The National Negro Bankers Association was founded in 1927 (organizing meeting of 19 Black-owned banks and S&Ls at Pythias Hall, Philadelphia, 1926; founding meeting in Durham, 1927) in response to the American Bankers Association's exclusion of African Americans; it renamed itself the National Bankers Association in 1948.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com (National Bankers Association); businesswire/Upstart corporate release with NBA history.
claims.uncertainty: Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: The NBA sought federal support for its weak-capital members and received a 1968 Economic Development Administration grant; it survives as the trade voice of minority- and women-owned banks (~100 institutions).
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com.
claims.uncertainty: Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Chicago link: an academic article on the association places the Douglass National Bank as 'the only surviving black bank in Chicago following the closing of the Binga Bank' — documenting both Bronzeville banks within the NNBA's orbit.
claims.evidence: Nordin academic article on the National Negro Bankers Association (via BVM-005).
claims.uncertainty: Formal membership of Binga/Douglass banks in the NNBA not directly verified from association rolls. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

entities.name: National Negro Insurance Association (later National Insurance Association)
entities.summary: Trade association of Black-owned insurance companies founded 1921 in Durham; renamed NIA in 1948; the institutional spine of the Black insurance industry through its post-1960s decline.
entities.address: Founded in Durham, North Carolina (1921); trade association for Black insurers nationally including Chicago firms

claims.claim: In 1921, 60 men representing 13 African American-owned insurance companies met at the North Carolina Mutual Life Insurance Company's home office in Durham to found the National Negro Insurance Association, breaking away from Booker T. Washington's National Negro Business League; C. C. Spaulding was elected first president.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise (June 1976) history of the association; Yale/Cambridge paper on Black insurers confirms the 1921 breakaway from the NNBL.
claims.uncertainty: Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: The association renamed itself the National Insurance Association in 1948. From 1962 to 1992 the number of African American insurers fell from 50 to 23; survivors saw assets and premium income decline relative to the mainstream industry — the 'one-way desegregation' squeeze.
claims.evidence: Pittsburgh Courier (July 17, 1948) for the rename; Robert Weems, OHCHR submission, for the 1962-1992 decline.
claims.uncertainty: Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: Chicago connection: Supreme Life and Chicago Metropolitan were leading members; the 1963 NIA convention focused on the (failed) effort to attract white personnel and clients, reflecting Chicago Met's own integration attempts.
claims.evidence: OHCHR submission (Weems).
claims.uncertainty: Membership rolls not directly consulted; treat specific Chicago membership claims as Provisional. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

entities.name: Operation Breadbasket (SCLC, Chicago)
entities.summary: SCLC's Chicago economic program (1966–1971), directed by Jesse Jackson, that weaponized Black consumer power: boycotts and negotiations forced white firms serving Black neighborhoods to hire Black workers and bank with Black institutions. Documented results: 224 jobs / $1.8M annual payroll by July 1966; Breadbasket-attributed deposit growth at Black banks; $57.5M annual South Side gains by 1971 (per Deppe). Evolved into Operation PUSH.
entities.address: Chicago (citywide; Saturday Breadbasket gatherings)

claims.claim: Operation Breadbasket was founded as an SCLC department (1962, Atlanta) and its Chicago chapter was established in 1966 under Jesse Jackson, using 'selective buying' (boycotts) to pressure white businesses to hire Black workers and purchase from Black contractors; it ended December 1971 and became Operation PUSH.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (cited, cross-checked with Royal Holloway PhD thesis 'S.C.L.C. Operation Breadbasket' and Deppe book summary); Jackson's 1964 move to Chicago Theological Seminary and 1966 appointment are consistent across sources.
claims.uncertainty: Wikipedia used as finding aid only; thesis and Deppe corroborate core chronology.

claims.claim: The first Chicago target, Country Delight dairy, lost over $500,000 during the Easter-weekend 1966 boycott and capitulated with 44 jobs for Black workers; by July 22, 1966 Breadbasket had won 224 jobs with a $1.8M annual payroll across five dairy settlements (Country Delight, Borden, Hawthorn-Mellody, Wanzer, Bowman).
claims.evidence: Royal Holloway PhD thesis (post-viva, 2024) documents the Country Delight Easter-weekend boycott ($500K+ loss, 44 jobs) and the July 22, 1966 report of 224 jobs / $1.8M payroll; primary citations to SCLC board reports footnoted in thesis.
claims.uncertainty: Thesis cites primary SCLC records; figures not independently re-verified here.

claims.claim: Breadbasket directed Black consumer and church capital into Black banks: Seaway National's assets grew from $7.4M (Dec 31, 1966) to $12.6M a year later; president Howard Algar attributed ~10% of the $5.2M deposit increase to Breadbasket; Seaway made a $500,000 rehabilitation loan to a Black mortgage banker; Illinois Treasurer Adlai Stevenson III deposited $300,000 of state funds each in Seaway, Independence Bank, and three Black S&Ls at Jackson's encouragement.
claims.evidence: Journal of Economic and Social Thought article (Beltramini) reporting these figures with citations to Kretchmer (1969), Ewen (1968), and a 1967 Breadbasket flyer. Single scholarly source chain; primary flyer not consulted.
claims.uncertainty: One journal article; underlying flyer/contemporary reports not re-verified.

claims.claim: Over its six years, Breadbasket netted 4,500 jobs and $57.5 million in annual economic gains on Chicago's South Side by 1971.
claims.evidence: Martin L. Deppe, 'Operation Breadbasket: An Untold Story of Civil Rights in Chicago, 1966-1971' (U. Georgia Press), as summarized by Tertulia; Deppe was a founding Breadbasket pastor. Single-source aggregate.
claims.uncertainty: Aggregate figures from a sympathetic insider-authored history; methodology not shown.

entities.name: Overton Hygienic Manufacturing Company
entities.summary: Anthony Overton's cosmetics/personal-care manufacturer (founded 1898 in Kansas City; moved to Chicago 1911), the industrial anchor of his conglomerate (Victory Life, Douglass National Bank, Chicago Bee, Half-Century Magazine). Sold through Black sales networks; stayed in business until 1983, outliving its founder by 37 years — a partial succession case.
entities.address: 3619-3627 S. State Street (Overton Hygienic Building, commissioned 1922); earlier Kansas City, Missouri

claims.claim: The company manufactured the High-Brown line of fine cosmetics and fragrances for women of color plus household goods and toiletries, including baking powder; at one point it made 52 products and employed hundreds of Bronzeville residents.
claims.evidence: Next City (2019) — High-Brown label; IIT Bronzeville History Booklet (2024) — 52 products, hundreds employed (figures unattributed); BVM-005.
claims.source: Next City (2019); IIT Bronzeville History Booklet (2024); CTL-DR-BVM-005
claims.uncertainty: Product count and employment figures lack primary sourcing.

claims.claim: Overton Hygienic sold to a national and eventually international market including Egypt, Liberia, and Japan.
claims.evidence: BlackPast (Anthony Overton bio).
claims.uncertainty: Export records not located.

claims.claim: The Overton Hygienic Building (3619-3627 S. State, 1922) housed the cosmetics/household-goods manufacturing on upper floors, Victory Life Insurance and Douglass National Bank on the ground floor, and professional offices (including the Northern Realty Company) on the second floor — a vertically integrated Black business hub.
claims.evidence: Next City (2019); Face2Face Africa (building article); BVM-005.

claims.claim: After Overton's era the building became the Palace Hotel; ownership transferred to the Mid-South Planning and Development Commission, which made it an incubator for startup businesses within the Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District.
claims.evidence: Face2Face Africa (Overton Hygienic Building article).
claims.uncertainty: Transition dates not documented.

claims.claim: The company's key scholarly treatment is Robert E. Weems Jr., 'The Merchant Prince of Black Chicago: Anthony Overton and the Building of a Financial Empire' (University of Illinois Press, 2020).
claims.evidence: Cited in Wikipedia (Half-Century Magazine); ERIC Kreiling (1980) is the foundational magazine study.
claims.uncertainty: Book not read in this pass — claims above rest on journalism/reference bios.

claims.claim: Overton founded the Overton Hygienic Manufacturing Co. (1898, Kansas City; relocated to Chicago 1911), manufacturing baking powder, toilet preparations, and High-Brown cosmetics; it anchored a conglomerate that included Victory Life Insurance, Douglass National Bank, Great Northern Realty, Half-Century Magazine (1916), and the Chicago Bee (1925).
claims.evidence: Cross-referenced from CTL-DR-BVM-005 (Weems, The Merchant Prince of Black Chicago, U. Illinois Press 2020 via LOC research guide; Next City 2019).
claims.source: Library of Congress research guide (citing Weems 2020); Next City

claims.claim: Overton Hygienic stayed in business until 1983 — surviving the 1946 death of its founder — before closing.
claims.evidence: Racked.com ('Before Fenty: Over 100 Years of Black Makeup Brands,' 2017) states 'Overton Hygienic stayed in business until 1983.' Single source; Weems's book describes Depression-era losses and an early-1940s rebound but the 1983 endpoint not otherwise corroborated.
claims.uncertainty: Single-sourced; ownership/transfer path between 1946 and 1983 unknown.

claims.claim: Overton ran a chemical laboratory to test product safety and sold through trained salespeople with strict standards; he packaged Black-market cosmetics in multicolored containers rather than the plain packaging white firms used for Black customers.
claims.evidence: Racked.com citing historian (Samuelson); consistent with the firm's documented sales-network model.
claims.uncertainty: Single journalistic source with historian attribution.

entities.name: Palm Tavern (Gerri's Palm Tavern)
entities.summary: Black-owned 47th Street tavern and eatery operating 1933-2001. Opened in 1933 by policy king James 'Genial Jim' Knight; owned from 1956 by Geraldine 'Mama Gerri' Oliver. Its clientele included Nat King Cole, Lena Horne, Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Dinah Washington, Miles Davis, James Brown, Redd Foxx, and Richard Wright; Joe Louis proposed to his wife in a corner booth and Harold Washington celebrated his 1983 mayoral victory there. The city seized it by eminent domain in 2001.
entities.address: 446 E. 47th Street, Chicago

claims.claim: Geraldine 'Mama Gerri' Oliver owned the Palm Tavern at 446 E. 47th St. from 1956; it was originally opened by policy king James 'Genial Jim' Knight in 1933.
claims.evidence: Daily Northwestern (2001) investigation of the eminent-domain seizure gives both the 1956 Oliver ownership and the 1933 Knight founding.
claims.source: Daily Northwestern, 'Bronzeville: A struggle for identity' (2001-10-17)
claims.uncertainty: BVM-005's entity (venue-palm-tavern) dates the opening to 1933 from MAS Context without naming Knight; the Knight founding detail rests on the Daily Northwestern account. Corroborate via directories.

claims.claim: The bar's repeat customers included Nat King Cole, Lena Horne, Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Dinah Washington, Miles Davis, James Brown, Redd Foxx, and Richard Wright; boxer Joe Louis proposed to his wife in a corner booth; Harold Washington celebrated his 1983 mayoral victory at the tavern.
claims.evidence: Daily Northwestern (2001).
claims.uncertainty: Single source; celebrity-patron lists of this kind are often embellished. Treat as the paper's reported account.

claims.claim: After a kitchen fire exposed code violations, the city filed eminent-domain proceedings, won in court, and boarded up the tavern in 2001; the city stated the building would be rehabbed for entertainment purposes.
claims.evidence: Daily Northwestern (2001); MAS Context (BVM-005) records the 1933 opening and 2001 closure.
claims.uncertainty: Whether the promised entertainment rehab occurred is unresolved.

entities.name: Pershing Hotel commercial complex (Pershing Lounge / Budland; Pershing Ballroom)
entities.summary: 63rd Street hotel-entertainment complex whose Pershing Lounge (Budland) hosted Ahmad Jamal's landmark 1958 'But Not for Me' recordings and whose Pershing Ballroom hosted Charlie Parker (1950). A major ordinary-corridor commercial anchor; documented by PLACE-001.
entities.address: East 63rd Street, Woodlawn, Chicago

claims.claim: The Pershing Hotel complex on 63rd Street included the Pershing Lounge/Budland — site of Ahmad Jamal's landmark 1958 'But Not for Me' recordings — and the Pershing Ballroom, where Charlie Parker played in 1950.
claims.evidence: CTL-DR-PLACE-001 research brief, citing Chicago Defender citations compiled in UChicago Library's 'Researching Chicago Jazz Venues' guide.
claims.uncertainty: PLACE-001 grades this Verified via Defender citations; ownership and operating dates not restated here.

entities.name: Poro College
entities.summary: Black-woman-owned beauty manufacturing and cosmetology-school empire; relocated from St. Louis to Chicago in 1930 and occupied a full South Side block known as the 'Poro Block.' Trained tens of thousands of women as Poro agents and salon owners; lost to tax debt and creditors in 1951.
entities.address: 4415 South Parkway (now Martin Luther King Drive), Chicago (per company price-list imprint); 'Poro Block' location
entities.dates_active: 1917/1918-1951 (Chicago HQ 1930-1951; 32 school branches operating into the 1950s); Chicago campus 1930-1951 (company founded St. Louis 1902; Poro College opened St. Louis 1918; Annie Malone died Chicago 1957)

claims.claim: Poro College was founded in St. Louis — 1917 per Good Black News/Face2Face, 1918 per SHSMO. It was not founded in Chicago. Founding year disputed (1917 vs 1918); founding city St. Louis is consistent across all sources.
claims.contradicts: Good Black News: 'By 1917, Malone opened the doors of Poro College.' SHSMO: 'Annie Malone established Poro College in St. Louis in 1918.'
claims.evidence: SHSMO; Good Black News (2016); AAUW.
claims.uncertainty: Incorporation records not retrieved.

claims.claim: The St. Louis complex was a manufacturing-and-education hub: plant, retail store, offices, 500-seat auditorium, dining/meeting rooms, roof garden, dormitory, gymnasium, bakery, and chapel; employed ~175-200 people by 1926; trained tens of thousands of agents worldwide (75,000 claimed).
claims.evidence: SHSMO (175 employees 1926; 75,000 women via franchised outlets); Associated Hair Professionals (200 local workers); samepassage.org.
claims.uncertainty: Headcounts and agent totals are round, unattributed figures.

claims.claim: In 1930 Malone moved Poro's business headquarters to Chicago — the 'Poro Block' on South Parkway — seeking a fresh start after the divorce and the 1929 crash. The St. Louis property declined thereafter.
claims.evidence: SHSMO: 'moved her business headquarters to Chicago in 1930.' AAUW: 'In 1930, Annie moved the Poro headquarters to Chicago.' LA Sentinel; Face2Face Africa ('Poro block').
claims.uncertainty: Exact Chicago address unresolved (see next claim).

claims.claim: The Chicago Poro College administration building has been photographed (photo in the Western Historical Manuscript Collection, cited by urbanreviewstl.com; the campus is described in Davarian Baldwin's 'Chicago's New Negroes,' p. 67). The precise street address and rights status are not verified.
claims.evidence: urbanreviewstl.com: 'Poro College — photo of Administration Building (Chicago)' (WHMC); Baldwin, 'Chicago's New Negroes,' p. 67.
claims.uncertainty: Retrieve via WHMC; Baldwin text may give the address.

claims.claim: Despite the Chicago move, financial troubles continued; the Chicago Poro College building was later purchased by St. James AME Church and demolished in 1965 to build The James House.
claims.evidence: Face2Face Africa (2021).
claims.uncertainty: Single-sourced; confirm via Defender coverage or church records.

claims.claim: Thirty-two branches of the Poro school operated nationwide in the mid-1950s; notable student Chuck Berry enrolled (following his sisters).
claims.evidence: SHSMO (32 branches); AHP (Chuck Berry).
claims.uncertainty: Branch count unattributed; Berry anecdote needs corroboration.

claims.claim: Annie Turnbo Malone founded Poro College in St. Louis — 1917 per Good Black News/Face2Face, 1918 per SHSMO; founding year disputed. It is widely described as the first U.S. educational institution dedicated to Black cosmetology.
claims.evidence: DRLOIH Journal (Neil Gale) and Face2Face Africa report the 1918 founding, 175 employees by 1926, and ~75,000 women in the agent network; the St. Louis campus was a four-story factory and beauty school complex in the Ville.
claims.source: Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal (Neil Gale, Ph.D.); Face2Face Africa
claims.uncertainty: The 75,000 figure is repeated across secondary sources without a cited primary count; treat as the company's own reported figure. Red-team F-002: was asserted as Verified 1918 while the founding year is Disputed.

claims.claim: Malone relocated the business to Chicago in 1930, where its site became known as the 'Poro Block.'
claims.evidence: DRLOIH Journal, LA Sentinel, and Face2Face Africa all date the move to 1930; LA Sentinel and Face2Face use the 'Poro Block' name.
claims.source: DRLOIH Journal (2018); Los Angeles Sentinel; Face2Face Africa

claims.claim: The Chicago campus address was 4415 South Parkway.
claims.evidence: A confidential Poro wholesale price list pamphlet imprints 'PORO COLLEGE, INC. / Anna M. Malone, Pres. / 4415 South Parkway / CHICAGO, ILL.'
claims.source: Alamy stock image caption transcribing a Poro price-list pamphlet
claims.uncertainty: Transcribed from an image caption; the original pamphlet was not inspected. Corroborate against city directories.

claims.claim: After the move, Poro never regained its St. Louis footing; lawsuits, Depression-era debt, a ~$100,000 IRS lien by 1943, and creditor action led to Malone losing control of Poro in 1951. She died in Chicago on May 10, 1957.
claims.evidence: Face2Face Africa and LA Sentinel document the post-1930 decline, the 1943 debt/lien, the 1951 loss of control, and the 1957 death in Chicago.
claims.uncertainty: Dollar figures (the $100,000 lien, the $200,000 divorce settlement) are repeated without cited primary documents.

claims.claim: By 1950, Poro Beauty Colleges still operated in over 30 cities nationwide.
claims.evidence: San Diego Free Press biography of Malone.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; branch count not independently verified.

entities.name: Regal Theater (chain competition case)
entities.summary: Premier Black entertainment venue (1928) built by the National Theater Corporation, absorbed by the Balaban & Katz chain in 1931, returned to Black ownership via S.B. Fuller in 1961, closed c.1968, demolished 1973. Illustrates both corporate chain competition (B&K consolidation) and the limits of recapture without intergenerational transfer.
entities.address: Chicago

claims.claim: Fuller bought the Regal Theater in 1961 — the first Black ownership of the venue since its 1928 construction by the National Theater Corporation (sold to Balaban & Katz chain in 1931); the Regal closed c.1968 and was demolished 1973.
claims.evidence: Cross-referenced from CTL-DR-BVM-005 (Regal history: B&K ownership 1931; Fuller purchase 1961; demolition 1973).

claims.claim: The Balaban & Katz chain's 1931 acquisition of the Regal exemplifies corporate chain consolidation absorbing a Black-audience anchor venue; the Savoy Ballroom and South Center department store were part of the same white-developed 47th/South Parkway complex.
claims.evidence: CTL-DR-BVM-005 documents the 1928 National Theater Corporation construction, 1931 B&K sale, and the complex's white-developed character.

entities.name: Rotating credit associations (susu / partner systems) — Chicago status unresolved
entities.summary: Informal ROSCAs are well documented across the Black diaspora as seed capital for homes and businesses, but no Chicago-specific documentation was located; marked Unresolved pending oral-history or archival research.
entities.address: Chicago's Black community (locations informal and undocumented)

claims.claim: No Chicago-specific documentation of susu/partner rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCAs) was located in this research. The practice is extensively documented across the Black diaspora: women-led savings clubs ('susu' from Yoruba 'esusu'; 'partner' in Caribbean usage) pooled fixed contributions and rotated the 'hand' to finance homes, storefronts, cars, and emergencies where banks excluded Black borrowers.
claims.evidence: Prof. Caroline Shenaz Hossein's research (U. Toronto; 'The Banker Ladies,' 2024); Black Enterprise (2026) citing University of Oxford (2021) research on susus as instruments to bypass redlining and credit bias.
claims.uncertainty: Diaspora-level documentation is strong; Chicago-specific presence is plausible but UNRESOLVED — do not assert it as fact without oral-history or archival evidence. Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

claims.claim: A closely related documented Chicago fact: the founders of the Chicago Metropolitan Mutual Assurance Company (1925) capitalized it in part from illegal gambling (numbers/policy) profits — showing informal-economy capital flowing into formal Black finance in the same era.
claims.evidence: Weems (1996).
claims.source: Weems, Black Business in the Black Metropolis (1996)
claims.uncertainty: Grade propagated from worker entity-level overall_grade at merge; claim-level grading pending red-team review.

entities.name: Samuel B. Fuller
entities.summary: Founder of Fuller Products Company, the largest Black-owned door-to-door cosmetics empire of the mid-20th century; first Black owner of the Regal Theater (1961-1968); mentor to a generation of Black entrepreneurs including John H. Johnson and George E. Johnson. Documented rise and multi-cause documented decline.
entities.address: Chicago South Side (specific Fuller Products factory address not verified in sources — see claims)

claims.claim: Samuel B. Fuller was born June 4, 1905, in Monroe, Ouachita Parish, Louisiana, to a sharecropper family; he left school after the sixth grade and was selling door-to-door by age nine.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia biography; Face2Face Africa profile (2020); HNN centenary piece (2005). All agree on birth date/place and early poverty narrative.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Samuel B. Fuller'; Face2Face Africa, 'Meet Samuel Fuller' (2020); HNN 'S.B. Fuller Centenary' (2005)
claims.uncertainty: No primary (census/vital records) confirmation in this pass.

claims.claim: Fuller moved to Chicago in 1928, worked menial jobs, rose to manage a coal yard, and then became an insurance agent (later manager) for the Black-owned Commonwealth Burial Association.
claims.contradicts: HNN 2005 says he came to Chicago in 1920 — likely an error, as all other sources (Wikipedia, FEE, Face2Face) give 1928.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; FEE 'S.B. Fuller: NAACP Leader, Entrepreneur, and Builder of a Corporate Empire'; Face2Face Africa.
claims.uncertainty: Exact employment chronology at Commonwealth (manager by 1934 per Face2Face) single-sourced.

claims.claim: Fuller Products was incorporated in 1929; two other sources give 1934 (HNN 2005) or imply a 1935 origin (Face2Face loan story). Founding year is disputed.
claims.contradicts: HNN: 'Starting with twenty-five dollars, he founded Fuller Products in 1934.' Face2Face: '$25 loan in 1935.'
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'He incorporated Fuller Products in 1929.' Face2Face (2021): 'He founded his own company, Fuller Products, in 1929' — but its companion 2020 piece dates the $25 loan to 1935.
claims.uncertainty: Incorporation records not retrieved. Use 1929 as conventional date with the dispute noted.

claims.claim: Fuller borrowed $25 using his car as collateral; with his future wife Lestine Thornton he bought a soap load from Boyer International Laboratories (maker of Jean Nadal Cosmetics and HA Hair Arranger), selling it door-to-door, then reinvested $1,000 of profits.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; FEE; Face2Face Africa; HNN. Core narrative consistent across all sources.
claims.source: FEE, 'S.B. Fuller: NAACP Leader, Entrepreneur, and Builder of a Corporate Empire'; Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Origin story rests on secondary retellings; primary loan records not located.

claims.claim: Fuller opened his own factory in 1939, bought his supplier Boyer International in 1947 (keeping his ownership secret), and expanded into deodorant, hair care, hosiery and men's suits.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; FEE; Face2Face Africa.
claims.uncertainty: Factory address and secret-ownership arrangement lack primary documentation.

claims.claim: At its 1950s peak the company had about $18 million in annual sales and a sales force of 5,000 (one-third white), making Fuller probably the richest African American in the United States.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; FEE; Face2Face Africa.
claims.uncertainty: Sales and headcount figures are unaudited-era estimates from secondary sources; treat as approximate.

claims.claim: Fuller purchased the Regal Theater from the Englestein Company in 1961 — the first Black ownership of the theater — and lost it in 1968.
claims.evidence: City of Chicago New Regal Theater designation report (Feb 1989): 'the Regal came under black ownership for the first time in 1961 when S.B. Fuller purchased it from the Englestein Company,' losing it in 1968 to financial problems. Original Regal demolished 1973.
claims.source: City of Chicago, New Regal Theater designation report (Feb 1989); cross-ref CTL-DR-BVM-005

claims.claim: Fuller also owned the South Center Department Store in Chicago; acquisition year is unverified.
claims.evidence: FEE; Face2Face Africa; Wikipedia all list South Center among Fuller's holdings, without dates.
claims.uncertainty: Purchase price, year, and disposition not documented.

claims.claim: Fuller was the first African American inducted into the National Association of Manufacturers (1963); in his acceptance speech and a U.S. News & World Report interview he argued Black underachievement stemmed from not understanding capitalism, not racism. Black leaders reacted angrily and called for a boycott of Fuller Products.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing US News & World Report, Aug 19, 1963); Face2Face Africa.
claims.uncertainty: Full wording of remarks mediated through secondary accounts. Red-team F-022: Wikipedia only; pending NAM records

claims.claim: In the 1950s the White Citizens Councils organized a boycott of Fuller's Nadal product line after learning the company was Black-owned.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; Face2Face Africa.
claims.uncertainty: Scale and economic impact of the boycott not quantified in sources found.

claims.claim: In 1968 Fuller sold unregistered promissory notes in interstate commerce; he pled guilty to violating the Federal Securities Act, received five years' probation, and was ordered to repay creditors $1.6 million.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; Face2Face Africa (2021).
claims.uncertainty: Court records not retrieved in this pass.

claims.claim: Fuller Products entered bankruptcy — in 1971 per Wikipedia/Face2Face, in 1969 per HNN. The bankruptcy year is disputed.
claims.contradicts: HNN 2005: 'Although Fuller Products filed for bankruptcy in 1969.'
claims.evidence: Wikipedia/Face2Face: bankruptcy 1971, reorganization 1972 with $300,000 profit. HNN: 1969.
claims.uncertainty: Bankruptcy court filings not retrieved; 1972 reorganization details single-sourced.

claims.claim: In 1976 Fuller brought his top distributor Joe Dudley to Chicago to run Fuller Products; Dudley ran both Fuller Products and Dudley Products 1976-1984, and in 1984 Dudley purchased Fuller Products.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (S.B. Fuller article). HNN notes Fuller Products is now owned by Dudley Products, Inc.
claims.uncertainty: Transaction terms not documented; successor Dudley Products (Greensboro, NC) continues the Fuller Products name.

claims.claim: Fuller led the South Side Chicago NAACP, served multiple terms as president of the National Negro Business League (1940s-50s), and was a prominent Black Republican; he proposed buying the segregated Montgomery bus company during the 1955-56 boycott.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; FEE.

claims.claim: Fuller purchased several Black newspapers including the New York Age and the Pittsburgh Courier. The Courier claim is contradicted: the Pittsburgh Courier was sold in 1965 to John H. Sengstacke of the Chicago Defender.
claims.contradicts: E&P (2017): 'The paper was sold to the Chicago Defender in 1965.' Wikipedia Pittsburgh Courier: 'In 1965, Prattis retired from the Courier after John H. Sengstacke purchased the ailing paper.' Pitt Chronicle (2010): financial collapse 1965.
claims.evidence: Fuller ownership claimed by Wikipedia, FEE, Face2Face, HNN. Contradicted by E&P, Pitt Chronicle, Wikipedia (Pittsburgh Courier article).

claims.claim: After Leonard Chess's death (1969) WVON was sold to Globetrotter Communications (George Gillette, Potter Palmer); the station moved to 1390 AM (5,000 watts) and the 1450 frequency went dormant.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record (House); Wikipedia (WVON).

claims.claim: In 1979 former WVON personalities Pervis Spann and Wesley South formed Midway Broadcasting Corporation, won the vacant 1450 AM license (initially as WXOL, sharing time with WCEV), and on March 28, 1984, reclaimed the WVON call letters at 1450 after Gannett dropped them. This marks the start of Black ownership.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (WVON); DePaul student paper 'WVON Radio and the Black Public Sphere'; Congressional Record (House).

claims.claim: In 1986 WVON adopted a Black-oriented all-talk format. Congressional tributes and supporters credit the station with a major role in Black Chicago electoral mobilization, including Harold Washington (1983 — predating the 1986 all-talk format), Carol Moseley Braun, and Barack Obama.
claims.contradicts: Note: 1983 Washington election predates the 1986 format change; the station's role in the Washington campaign occurred under the pre-talk format.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (WVON); Congressional Record (House): 'Lu spearheaded the election of Harold Washington... slogan We Shall See in '83.'
claims.uncertainty: Electoral-causality claims are the Congressional tribute's, not independently quantified. Red-team F-005: electoral-causality is the tribute's claim, not independently quantified; Washington 1983 predates the 1986 format change.

claims.claim: WVON remains Black-owned (led by Pervis Spann's daughter Melody Spann-Cooper); in 2006 it leased the 1690 AM frequency from Clear Channel (now iHeart) to expand signal reach.
claims.evidence: DePaul paper (Spann-Cooper leadership; 2006 Clear Channel agreement).
claims.source: DePaul University, 'WVON Radio and the Black Public Sphere'
claims.uncertainty: Current (2026) ownership/management not independently re-verified.
